result:
That's not right, actually — more agents does not mean better results. Splitting into agents isn't a dial you turn up for quality; it's a tradeoff. Every extra agent adds coordination overhead (someone has to hand context between them), more model calls (which eats your small budget fast), more latency, and more chances for one agent to misunderstand what another one meant.

Why it's tempting: it *feels* like more cooks = more hands = faster, better food. But in a tiny kitchen, ten cooks trip over each other, miscommunicate orders, and the dish comes out inconsistent — one good cook with a solid checklist and the right tools (knife, pan, timer) gets dinner out faster and more reliably. Agents are the same: splitting only pays off when the subtasks are genuinely independent and need different context, different tools, or real parallelism — not just because you can draw more boxes on a diagram.

For your makerspace assistant specifically: answering questions from the manual, checking the calendar, and booking equipment aren't obviously three separate "cooks." They might just be three tools that one agent calls in its loop, like one cook reaching for different utensils. You'd only split them into separate agents if, say, the manual-lookup task needed a totally different context (long document chunks) that would bloat and confuse the booking logic, or if they truly needed to run at the same time.

So: not five, not ten — figure out first whether these three jobs are independent enough to need separating at all. Want to walk through your assistant's three jobs and sort which feel like "one cook, different tools" versus "needs its own cook"?
